newsitem.title: NIGERIA: Oil-producing Nigeria groans under fuel scarcity.
newsitem.headline: Oil-producing Nigeria groans under fuel scarcity.

text.p: Fuel scarcity which has gripped Nigeria in intermittent spells this year is worsening and with the spells getting longer, manufacturers have warned of the imminent collapse of industries.

"The first six months of this year have been lost (to fuel scarcity). It has had negative multi-dimensional impact on manufacturers," Uzor Okeke, director of the Manufacturers Association of Nigeria (MAN), said in Lagos on Thursday.
He said the scarcity had coincided with the "worst-ever performance" of the state electricity utility, National Electric Power Authority (NEPA).

"We are a laughing stock throughout the world because 'oil-rich' Nigeria can't deliver ordinary petrol to its citizens," said the Civil Liberties Organisation, the leading human rights group, in newspaper advertisements on Friday.
For more than two weeks Lagos, the hub of Nigerian business, has suffered a fuel shortage which in recent days has spread to the government capital Abuja.

Long queues have become a common feature at any petrol station dispensing fuel, while a black market is booming with people paying as much 4,000 naira ($47) for a 50-litre (10 gallon) can of petrol, more than seven times the normal price.
The bitter irony of fuel shortages in Africa's biggest oil producer has not been lost on a local press which has dubbed it a "national shame".

Okeke said manufacturers, besides incurring additional production costs, were having difficulty distributing their products to consumers, who on their part were finding their diminished purchasing power further threatened by high fuel costs.

He said manufacturers were also not reassured by the contradictory explanations offered by government officials for the scarcity, including aging refineries, non-compliance with refinery maintenance schedules and non-disbursement of budgeted funds for the refineries by the federal authorities.

"You cannot pinpoint the cause of the present problems from official statements," said Okeke, "which means there has been no concerted effort on the part of government officials to comprehend the cause of the problem."
MAN proposed in the short term that the govertnment should allow independent oil marketing companies to import refined petroleum to ease the scarcity and avert the imminent collapse of industries.
But in the long-term, he said the government should privatise Nigeria's four refineries and NEPA.

"Under a privatised economy there will be sanctions against inefficiency. This will further promote the fortunes of the various sectors of the economy as better management of resources will evolve," he said.
Nigeria, a major player in the Organisation of Petroleum Exporting Countries (OPEC), produces roughly two million barrels a day (bpd) of crude oil.
Of this, 250,000 bpd is allocated to four refineries with a combined capacity to process 445,000 bpd of crude, but they are currently operating well below that.
